concepts.name: Abhinav Bharat Society: Founding, Structure, and Ideological Foundations
key_dimensions: Founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar in 1904 at Nasik — distinguishing it from Bal Gangadhar Tilak's broader extremism
Inspired by Mazzini's 'Young Italy' movement — tracing the European revolutionary influence on Indian nationalism
Secret society model vs. open political agitation — contrast with INC methods of the same period
Role of Shyamji Krishna Varma and India House, London as ideological and logistical support network

concepts.name: Anushilan Samiti: Dual Centers, Factionalism, and Organizational Evolution
key_dimensions: Calcutta Anushilan Samiti (founded 1902 by Promotha Mitter) vs. Dhaka Anushilan Samiti (founded 1906 by Pulin Das) — key distinction UPSC exploits
Transition from physical culture/gymnasium fronts to armed revolutionary cells — phases of organizational evolution
Barindra Kumar Ghosh's role in radicalizing the Calcutta branch toward bomb-making and political assassinations
Network of akhadas as cover organizations — comparison with Abhinav Bharat's secret cell model

concepts.name: Ideological Roots: Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay and Religious Nationalism as Revolutionary Fuel
key_dimensions: Anushilana (self-cultivation) philosophy drawn from Bankim's writings — 'Ananda Math' and 'Vande Mataram' as ideological texts
Synthesis of Hindu revivalism and armed resistance — distinguishing religious nationalism from Gandhian spiritualism
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's influence: Shivaji festivals and Ganesh Puja as mass mobilization precursors to revolutionary activity
UPSC trap: Differentiating 'cultural nationalism' of Bankim from 'political revolutionary nationalism' of Savarkar

concepts.name: Alipore Bomb Case (1908–1909): Significance, Outcomes, and Legal Dimensions
key_dimensions: Immediate trigger: Muzaffarpur bombing (1908) by Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki — mistaken identity dimension
Arrest of Bal Gangadhar Tilak separately vs. Aurobindo Ghosh's arrest in Alipore — convergence of extremist and revolutionary tracks
Aurobindo Ghosh's acquittal and subsequent spiritual withdrawal — impact on revolutionary movement's leadership vacuum
Significance as the first major sedition-conspiracy trial targeting organized revolutionary networks in India

concepts.name: Khudiram Bose and the Muzaffarpur Bombing: Symbolism and Revolutionary Martyrdom
key_dimensions: First major bombing attempt by revolutionary nationalists in Bengal — marking tactical shift from individual assassination to bomb warfare
Target: Magistrate Kingsford (who had flogged Sushil Sen) — personal grievance fused with political resistance
Khudiram Bose's execution at age 18 — youngest revolutionary martyr, propaganda value for the movement
Prafulla Chaki's suicide upon arrest — comparison with later revolutionary martyrdom narratives (Bhagat Singh era)

concepts.name: Savarkar's India House and the London Revolutionary Network
key_dimensions: India House as a hub connecting Indian students in London with revolutionary ideology — Shyamji Krishna Varma's patronage
Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' — banned immediately, significance as first nationalist reinterpretation of 1857
Arms smuggling network: Browning pistols sent to India — linking London operations to Nasik conspiracy
Madan Lal Dhingra's assassination of Curzon Wyllie (1909) — India House's direct link to political violence in Britain

concepts.name: Nasik Conspiracy Case (1910) and Savarkar's Extradition Trial
key_dimensions: Assassination of Collector A.M.T. Jackson by Anant Laxman Kanhere — Abhinav Bharat's direct operational act
Savarkar's arrest, transportation to India, and the 'Marseilles escape attempt' (1910) — international legal dimensions
The Hague Arbitration Tribunal ruling on Savarkar's extradition — rare instance of international law in colonial Indian history
Two life sentences ('double transportation for life') — UPSC frequently tests this specific punishment detail

concepts.name: Pulin Das and the Dhaka Anushilan Samiti: Organizational Reach and Distinct Character
key_dimensions: Dhaka branch's more extensive rural network compared to Calcutta branch's urban intellectual character
Partition of Bengal (1905) as catalyst for radicalization of the Dhaka Samiti
Pulin Das's emphasis on physical training, lathi practice, and armed cadre — distinct from Barindra Ghosh's bomb-making focus
UPSC trap: Conflating Dhaka and Calcutta Anushilan Samitis as one organization — they were ideologically and operationally distinct

concepts.name: Aurobindo Ghosh's Revolutionary Phase: Bridge Between Extremism and Armed Resistance
key_dimensions: Aurobindo's dual role: Editor of 'Yugantar' and 'Karmayogin' + covert support to Barindra's revolutionary group
Doctrine of 'Passive Resistance' in his political writings vs. actual complicity in bomb conspiracy — the ideological-operational gap
Chittaranjan Das's defense argument in Alipore trial — legally significant speech on Indian nationalism
Pondicherry withdrawal (1910): whether political retreat or genuine spiritual transformation — a recurring analytical question

concepts.name: Yugantar and Kal: Revolutionary Press as Ideological Weapon
key_dimensions: Yugantar (1906) edited by Bhupendranath Dutta and Barindra Kumar Ghosh — first explicitly revolutionary newspaper in Bengal
Content analysis: justification of political violence, critique of moderate nationalism, anti-colonial armed resistance doctrine
British response: Sedition prosecutions, press censorship under the Newspaper (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908
Comparison with Tilak's 'Kesari' — both sedition targets but different in explicitness of revolutionary content

concepts.name: Government Repression: Seditious Meetings Act, Criminal Law Amendment Act, and Their Impact
key_dimensions: Seditious Meetings Act (1907) and Prevention of Seditious Meetings Act — direct legislative response to revolutionary activity
Criminal Law Amendment Act (1908) — targeting Anushilan Samiti's organizational networks specifically
Deportation without trial: Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh (1907) — state's use of Regulation III of 1818
Impact analysis: Did repression destroy or disperse/radicalize the revolutionary movement? — key evaluative question

concepts.name: Bharat Mata Society and Savarakar's Philosophical Contribution to Revolutionary Nationalism
key_dimensions: Bharat Mata Society as precursor to Abhinav Bharat — continuity of Savarkar's organizational building
Savarkar's concept of 'Hindutva' emerging from revolutionary nationalism — tracing the ideological evolution
Distinction between Savarkar's territorial/ethnic nationalism and Congress's civic nationalism
UPSC trap: Savarkar's early revolutionary phase often conflated with his later Hindutva ideology — these are distinct phases

concepts.name: Revolutionary Nationalism and the Role of the Diaspora: Shyamji Krishna Varma and Madame Cama
key_dimensions: Shyamji Krishna Varma: founding of India House, 'The Indian Sociologist' journal — London as revolutionary base
Madame Bhikaiji Cama: unfurling Indian flag at Stuttgart Socialist International (1907) — first international display
Paris Indian Society and its connections to Abhinav Bharat — transnational revolutionary network
Comparison: Diaspora revolutionaries vs. home-based revolutionaries — resource access, ideological independence, limitations

concepts.name: Relationship Between Extremist Politics and Revolutionary Nationalism: Overlap and Divergence
key_dimensions: Lal-Bal-Pal's 'extremism' within INC vs. Savarkar/Anushilan Samiti's extra-constitutional revolutionary path — critical distinction
Tilak's support for Shivaji's legacy vs. Savarkar's armed conspiracy — where admiration ends and complicity begins
Both streams rejected Moderates' petitioning but diverged on organized violence as a legitimate tool
UPSC trap: Classifying Tilak as a 'revolutionary' — he was an extremist within constitutional politics, not a conspirator

concepts.name: Revolutionary Nationalism and Women: Participation, Limitations, and Symbolic Roles
key_dimensions: Limited but notable participation: women as couriers, shelter providers, and occasionally armed participants
Madame Cama as the most prominent female figure — her role as symbol vs. organizational leader
Ideological contradiction: Revolutionary groups drew on Hindu revivalist imagery (Bharat Mata) but had patriarchal organizational structures
Comparison with later revolutionary movements (HSRA) — did female participation expand significantly?

concepts.name: The Ghadar Party Connection: Bridging Bengal Revolutionaries and Punjab-Based Diaspora Militancy
key_dimensions: Anushilan Samiti's influence on Ghadar Party ideology — transmission of revolutionary thought to North America
Lala Hardayal's intellectual bridge between Bengal revolutionary tradition and Ghadar militancy
Ghadar Movement (1913–1915) as an attempt at armed uprising — why it failed despite revolutionary fervor
UPSC frequently tests the Ghadar Party's founding location (San Francisco, 1913) and its newspaper 'Ghadar'

concepts.name: Decline of Abhinav Bharat and Anushilan Samiti: Causes and Legacy Assessment
key_dimensions: Internal factors: police infiltration, leadership arrests, lack of mass base, ideological isolation
External factors: World War I emergency powers, Rowlatt Act atmosphere, emergence of Gandhian mass movement
Savarkar's formal dissolution of Abhinav Bharat in 1952 — the organization's surprisingly long dormant existence
Legacy debate: Did revolutionary terrorism achieve anything? — Bipin Chandra's critique vs. nationalists' valorization

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: Bengal Revolutionary Nationalism vs. Punjab Revolutionary Nationalism (HSRA)
key_dimensions: Bengal tradition (1900s–1910s): Hindu revivalist ideology, bomb-making, secret societies — vs. Punjab/HSRA (1920s–1930s): socialist ideology, open martyrdom strategy
Bhagat Singh's explicit critique of religious nationalism — marking ideological evolution from Bengal school
Organizational comparison: Anushilan's cell-based secrecy vs. HSRA's propaganda-through-action approach
Both traditions' selective use of violence: targeted assassination vs. symbolic bombing (Central Assembly, 1929)

concepts.name: Historiographical Debates on Revolutionary Nationalism: Colonial Records vs. Nationalist Historiography
key_dimensions: Colonial characterization as 'terrorism' vs. nationalist historians' framing as 'armed resistance' — the naming controversy
Bipin Chandra's assessment: revolutionaries lacked mass base and theoretical framework — a mainstream critical view
Revisionist views: Sumit Sarkar's nuanced analysis of Bengal revolutionary tradition in 'Modern India'
UPSC application: Questions asking to 'critically examine the contribution of revolutionary nationalists' require this multi-perspective framework
